title: Consulting on the Cusp of Disruption
pub: Harvard Business Review, October 2013, at 106 (reprint R1310F)
author: Clayton M. Christensen · Dina Wang · Derek van Bever

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Disruption theory: Historical examples weakly fit predictions
st.an: The source treats disruption theory as broadly applicable and confidently predicts disruption in professional services, including law and consulting. Although it concedes that consulting’s exact trajectory cannot be forecast, it does not engage the cluster’s evidence that historical cases weakly conform to the theory or that professional-service indicators do not establish inevitable displacement.
qs: If our long study of disruption has led us to any universal conclusion, it is that every industry will eventually face it.
Finally, although we cannot forecast the exact progress of disruption in the consulting industry, we can say with utter confidence that whatever its pace, some incumbents will be caught by surprise.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core logic that technology is most applicable to routinized, well-defined work while complex, interdependent professional judgment remains durable. It materially extends the synthesis by specifying how incumbents can redesign around this selective frontier: modularize and productize suitable services, adopt distinct profit models, and protect autonomous growth units from the core organization. Its claims are primarily about consulting and are partly predictive, with legal services used as an analogue rather than direct evidence of current legal-AI performance.
qs: This approach is most pertinent for consulting jobs that have been routinized—that is, the process for uncovering a solution is well-known and the scope of the solution is fairly well defined.
**A new profit model.** In most cases it will reflect priorities different from those of the core business.

st.t: Business disruption: Incumbents must separate experiments credibly
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition: disruption is a business-model and organisational challenge, not a consequence of technology adoption alone. It argues that incumbent resource-allocation logic obstructs renewal and prescribes genuinely autonomous units with protected funding, distinct economics and senior leadership support, while treating the timing and form of consulting disruption as uncertain.
qs: As we teach our Harvard Business School students, the resources, processes, and priorities that an organization acquires and develops for its initial success become sea anchors when it attempts to change course.
**A separate resource allocation process.** This will fund the unit regardless of the fortunes of the core business.

st.t: Corporate buyers: Insourcing and partnerships coexist
st.an: The source supports the proposition that informed corporate buyers gain control by unbundling and selectively allocating work, while law firms remain involved in premium and lead-counsel roles. Its emphasis is more strongly on competitive pressure and weakened incumbent advantages than on stable partnerships, but it expressly describes coordinated delivery rather than wholesale firm displacement.
qs: By now corporate general counsel are well along in the process of disaggregating traditional law firms, taking advantage of new competitors such as Axiom and Lawyers on Demand, which reduce costs and increase efficiency through technology, streamlined workflow, and alternative staffing models.
LeClairRyan coordinates this discovery work with the higher-value services of lead counsel, who focus on the less routine aspects of litigation.

st.t: Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition that increasingly capable corporate buyers disaggregate legal work, allocating routine components to lower-cost or alternative providers while retaining lead counsel for less routine, higher-value work. It also supports pressure toward nonhourly billing and greater price competition, though these are presented partly as survey expectations and it does not address AI-specific training or verification risks.
qs: By now corporate general counsel are well along in the process of disaggregating traditional law firms, taking advantage of new competitors such as Axiom and Lawyers on Demand, which reduce costs and increase efficiency through technology, streamlined workflow, and alternative staffing models.
LeClairRyan coordinates this discovery work with the higher-value services of lead counsel, who focus on the less routine aspects of litigation.

kp.k: Disruption theory frames consulting and legal market change
kp.d: The authors argue in 2013 that consulting is beginning to experience disruption already visible in law: entrants with different business models improve sufficiently to challenge incumbents, which may initially ignore them or retreat upmarket. Their investigation included conversations with more than 50 incumbent and emerging firm leaders, clients, academics and researchers, and a May 2013 HBS roundtable. This is a theory-led interpretation and forecast, not a demonstrated account of completed disruption.
qs: We’ve spoken extensively with more than 50 leaders of incumbent and emerging firms, their clients, and academics and researchers who study them.

The pattern of industry disruption is familiar: New competitors with new business models arrive; incumbents choose to ignore the new players or to flee to higher-margin activities; a disrupter whose product was once barely good enough achieves a level of quality acceptable to the broad middle of the market, undermining the position of longtime leaders and often causing the “flip” to a new basis of competition.

kp.k: Opacity and agility historically protected professional service incumbents
kp.d: The authors identify two protections: clients struggle to assess specialized advice both before and after engagements, making reputation and price substitutes for measurable quality; human-capital-based firms with limited fixed investment can adapt readily. They argue these protections are eroding, rather than suggesting that technology alone explains disruption.
qs: Their reaction is understandable, because two factors—opacity and agility—have long made consulting immune to disruption.
Price is often seen as a proxy for quality, buoying the premiums charged by name-brand firms.
Their primary assets are human capital and their fixed investments are minimal; they aren’t hamstrung by substantial resource allocation decisions.

kp.k: Different business models monetize different kinds of work
kp.d: The article distinguishes judgment-based solution shops handling undefined problems and charging fee-for-service, value-added process businesses delivering repeatable work of defined scope and charging for output, and facilitated networks charging intermediation fees. This taxonomy underpins its argument that integrated professional-service offerings can be separated into differently organized businesses.
qs: The traditional solution-shop model is at risk of being disrupted by other models.
Delivers value primarily through consultants’ judgment rather than through repeatable processes
Structured to address problems of defined scope with standard processes
Customers pay fees to the network, which in turn pays the service provider

kp.k: Strategy work and billing practices showed changing demand
kp.d: Tom Rodenhauser of Kennedy Consulting Research & Advisory is the attributed source for classic strategy declining from 60%–70% of traditional strategy firms’ work roughly 30 years earlier to about 20%. Separately, an unnamed large-firm partner predicted value-based pricing would rise from high single digits to one-third of projects within 20 years; this is an interviewee's expectation, not an observed pricing outcome.
qs: At traditional strategy-consulting firms, the share of work that is classic strategy is now about 20%—down from 60% to 70% some 30 years ago.

We spoke to a partner at one large firm who anticipates that the percentage of projects employing value-based pricing instead of per diem billing will go from the high single digits to a third of the business within 20 years.

kp.k: In-house capability and financial transparency weakened law-firm opacity
kp.d: The authors trace reduced corporate dependence on law firms to the development of the modern corporate law function, exemplified by Ben Heineman at GE about 25 years before publication. They report general counsel budgets representing about one-third of America's $500 billion legal market and argue that Am Law 100 financial rankings, including leverage and profits per partner, enabled comparisons previously unavailable to clients.
qs: Today general counsel budgets account for about one-third of the $500 billion legal market in America.
By adding increasingly granular data, such as leverage and profits per partner, the Am Law rankings shone a light on the previously secretive operations of white-shoe firms.

kp.k: Alternative providers and performance information enable legal unbundling
kp.d: The article describes corporate general counsel allocating work to providers such as Axiom and Lawyers on Demand that combine technology, streamlined workflows and alternative staffing. AdvanceLaw is reported to vet firms and independent practitioners and share performance information with 90 general counsel. Panasonic North America GC Bob Marin credits increased transparency with better work allocation; David Wilkins is separately credited with observing that GCs increasingly identify with corporate executives rather than outside counsel.
qs: By now corporate general counsel are well along in the process of disaggregating traditional law firms, taking advantage of new competitors such as Axiom and Lawyers on Demand, which reduce costs and increase efficiency through technology, streamlined workflow, and alternative staffing models.

His business vets firms and independent practitioners for quality, efficiency, and client service and shares performance information with its membership of 90 general counsel from major global companies, including Google, Panasonic, Nike, and eBay.
Today’s general counsel increasingly view their fellow corporate executives, rather than outside counsel, as their peer group.

kp.k: Discovery and temporary staffing illustrate legal delivery restructuring
kp.d: At publication, LeClairRyan reportedly employed more than 300 full-time and contract lower-cost, highly trained lawyers in its Discovery Solutions Practice, separating large-scale review from lead counsel's less routine litigation work. Freshfields Continuum, launched in mid-2012, used alumni as temporary attorneys to absorb demand fluctuations. These are historical examples of task and staffing reorganization, not evidence of AI-driven displacement.
qs: For example, LeClairRyan is a full-service U.S. firm that currently employs more than 300 (full-time and contract) lower-cost but highly trained lawyers in its Discovery Solutions Practice.
LeClairRyan coordinates this discovery work with the higher-value services of lead counsel, who focus on the less routine aspects of litigation.

Freshfields Continuum employs alumni as attorneys on a temporary basis to meet fluctuations in demand as “a solution for efficient head count management,” according to the Freshfields partner Tim Jones.

kp.k: Legal surveys recorded expectations of sustained market restructuring
kp.d: An AdvanceLaw survey found 52% of GCs agreed and 28% disagreed that temporary contract attorney use would increase; 79% expected more unbundling. Altman Weil's surveys of managing partners and chairs recorded expected price competition rising from 42% in 2009 to 92% in 2012, and belief in fewer equity partners and more nonhourly billing as permanent trends rising from less than 30% each to 68% and 80%, respectively. Another cited AdvanceLaw result was that 72% of GCs intended to move more work away from white-shoe firms. These measure expectations or intentions, not realized changes; respondent counts are not provided.
qs: An AdvanceLaw survey of general counsel found that 52% agree (and only 28% disagree) with the statement that general counsel “will make greater use of temporary contract attorneys,” and 79% agree that “unbundling of legal services…will rise.”

The legal management consultancy Altman Weil, surveying law firm managing partners and chairs, found that in 2009 only 42% expected to see more price competition, whereas by 2012 that number had climbed to 92%.
Similarly, in 2009 less than 30% thought fewer equity partners and more nonhourly billing were permanent trends; in 2012 their numbers had reached 68% and 80%, respectively.
In a recent survey by AdvanceLaw, 72% of general counsel said that they will be migrating a larger percentage of work away from white-shoe firms.

kp.k: Consulting alumni strengthen buyers and encourage insourcing
kp.d: Kennedy Research estimates annual turnover of 18%–20% across levels at prestigious consultancies. The authors report 27,000 McKinsey alumni versus 21,000 in 2007 and nearly 50,000 across the Big Three. They link clients' hiring of former consultants to narrower outsourced scopes, more active resource management and insourcing, while explicitly acknowledging the lack of precise public data on corporate hiring. Cost aggregation and procurement scrutiny further undermine price as a quality proxy.
qs: Kennedy Research estimates that turnover at all levels in prestigious consulting firms averages 18% to 20% a year.
McKinsey alone has 27,000 alumni today, up from 21,000 in 2007; the alumni of the Big Three combined are approaching 50,000.

Precise data are not publicly available, but we know that many companies have hired small armies of former consultants for internal strategy groups and management functions, which contributes to the companies’ increasing sophistication about consulting services.
They have moved more and more work in-house, such as average costing analysis, an exercise that once racked up billable hours.

kp.k: Knowledge democratization shifts competition toward specialized modular providers
kp.d: The authors use modularization theory to explain clients replacing one-stop solution shops with specialists when integrated services contain costly features they do not value. Market research firms, expert networks and database providers take over information gathering, reducing opacity and incumbent differentiation; some then move upmarket into advice based on their research.
qs: The shift is generally triggered when customers realize that they are paying too much for features they don’t value and that they want greater speed, responsiveness, and control.
As access to knowledge is democratized, opacity fades and clients no longer have to pay the fees of big consulting firms.
Some of these modular providers are moving upmarket by providing their own boutique consulting services, offering advice based on the research they specialize in gathering.

kp.k: Freelance consulting networks reduce overhead and increase client control
kp.d: Eden McCallum and Business Talent Group assemble lean teams, largely midlevel and senior alumni of leading consultancies, using external research rather than proprietary knowledge development. Their cost advantage comes from avoiding unstaffed time, costly offices, recruiting and training. Drawing partly on Heidi Gardner's study of Eden McCallum, the authors describe greater experience and client control, expecting these models to appeal particularly for well-defined, lower-risk work. They acknowledge that expansion might eventually require incumbent-like costs.
qs: These firms assemble leaner project teams of freelance consultants (mostly midlevel and senior alumni of top consultancies) for clients at a small fraction of the cost of traditional competitors.
They can achieve these economies in large part because they do not carry the fixed costs of unstaffed time, expensive downtown real estate, recruiting, and training.
We expect these attributes to be particularly compelling when projects are better defined and the value at risk is not great enough to justify the price of a prestigious consultancy.

kp.k: Asset-based consulting separates revenue from project staffing
kp.d: McKinsey Solutions, originating in business-model innovations initiated in 2007, embeds software and analytics in clients rather than relying solely on finite staffed engagements. The authors suggest shorter projects, clearer ROI, recurring engagement and lead generation as commercial benefits, and interpret it as a hedge against disruption. More generally, asset-based consulting packages intellectual property into technology, typically requiring less human intervention and using subscription or license fees, especially for repeatable, data-heavy work requiring frequent updates.
qs: McKinsey Solutions marked the first time the consultancy unbundled its offerings and focused so heavily on hard knowledge assets.
McKinsey Solutions is intended to provide a strong hedge against potential disruption.

The amount of human intervention and customization varies, but in general it’s less than what the traditional consulting model requires, meaning lower expenses spread out over a longer period of time (usually through a subscription or license-based fee).
This approach is most pertinent for consulting jobs that have been routinized—that is, the process for uncovering a solution is well-known and the scope of the solution is fairly well defined.

kp.k: AI and analytics are expected to accelerate productization
kp.d: The article describes Narrative Science using AI algorithms to analyze data and deliver readable insights. It predicts improving AI and big-data capabilities will expand productization, while stating that only a limited number of consulting jobs could then be productized. It also asserts that BeyondCore's automated analysis and animated briefings render the junior analyst role obsolete, without presenting workforce measurements; Motista is offered as an example of lower-priced software-generated customer insights. These claims concern consulting analytics, not measured effects on junior lawyers.
qs: One example is Narrative Science, which uses artificial intelligence algorithms to run analytics and extract key insights that are then delivered to clients in easy-to-read form.
Only a limited number of consulting jobs can currently be productized, but that will change as consultants develop new intellectual property.
We expect that as artificial intelligence and big data capabilities improve, the pace of productization will increase.

The big data company BeyondCore can automatically evaluate vast amounts of data, identify statistically relevant insights, and present them through an animated briefing, rendering the junior analyst role obsolete.

kp.k: Disruption may consolidate incumbents without eliminating premium advice
kp.d: The authors predict top-tier consolidation and more M&A as firms seek resources, intellectual property and missing capabilities. They nevertheless expect complex, interdependent, high-stakes matters to retain premium bespoke advisers, partly because prestigious brands reassure boards. They forecast a shrinking range of problems requiring such solutions as entrants improve, with disruption beginning among smaller and previously unserved clients rather than the largest accounts. They explicitly qualify that disruption is a process whose precise course cannot be known.
qs: Disruption is, after all, a process, not an event, and it does not necessarily mean all-out destruction.
However disruption unfolds, a core of critical work will survive, requiring custom solutions to complex, interdependent problems across industries and geographies.
But as disrupters march upmarket, armed with leaner business models and new technology, the range of problems requiring strategic solutions should shrink.
While consulting’s core apparatus is focused on bigger and bigger client engagements, small customers are unguarded.

kp.k: Cross-disciplinary providers can counter modularization with integrated solutions
kp.d: The authors argue that blurred professional boundaries also create interdependent problems favoring hard-to-imitate combinations of capabilities. Axiom exemplifies an alternative legal service provider moving beyond contract staffing into advising GCs on cost and quality, combining lawyers, management consultants, workflow specialists and technologists. IDEO and diversified professional-service firms provide parallel examples. The article describes Big Four expansion into management consulting but leaves open whether they will disrupt incumbent models or copy them.
qs: The legal services provider Axiom has expanded far beyond its roots in contract lawyer staffing to advising general counsel on substantive ways to lower costs while maintaining quality.
To that end, Axiom now deploys a mix of lawyers, management consultants, workflow specialists, and technologists.
By spanning domains and creating models that are hard to pick apart, these companies are effectively fighting modularization.
Whether they’ll attempt to create a disruptive business model or just copy the incumbents’ business model remains to be seen.

kp.k: Quantifiable analytics could weaken brand-based competitive barriers
kp.d: The authors predict that increasingly capable predictive technology and automation will change consultants' activities and value. They argue that faster, quantifiable outputs reduce opacity and may weaken brand barriers, potentially benefiting emerging-market firms such as Tata Consultancy Services and Infosys. Existing automation and insourcing of costing and pricing, and automation of customer relationship analysis, are presented as precursors rather than evidence that all advisory work can be automated.
qs: Average costing and pricing analysis have been automated and increasingly insourced; now Salesforce.com and others are automating customer relationship analysis.

Their speed and quantifiable output help reduce, and perhaps even negate, brand-based barriers to growth; thus they might accelerate the success of emerging-market consulting firms such as Tata Consultancy Services and Infosys.

kp.k: Self-disruption requires organizational separation and sustained leadership protection
kp.d: The authors recommend an autonomous unit, leaders with relevant experience, separate resource allocation, independent sales channels, a different profit model and unwavering CEO commitment. They argue that separation alone cannot remove the incumbent's embedded allocation priorities. For McKinsey Solutions, the test is whether the partnership tolerates competition with its engagement business, including clients seeking technology without a full consulting team.
qs: The unit should have all the functional skills it needs to succeed, freeing it from reliance on the parent organization, and it must not report to the business or businesses that are being disrupted.
A separate resource allocation process.
Independent sales channels.
A new profit model.
Unwavering commitment by the CEO.
Will the partnership blink when a nontraditional client requests delivery of McKinsey Solutions without obligatory use of a full engagement team?

kp.k: Buyers and providers should actively reassess sourcing and value
kp.d: The article recommends that buyers periodically assess provider markets, aggregate spending, demand transparency in underlying analysis, consider reusable knowledge assets, involve staff with professional-services experience and use outcomes-based assessments to guide hiring. Providers are encouraged to track changing needs, procurement involvement, specialized rivals, technology-enabled partners and the profitability of smaller projects as warning signs of disruption.
qs: Do your providers make transparent the analyses that underpin their recommendations? Do you have an opportunity to standardize any of these analyses into hard assets that you can maintain?
Do you have a robust, outcomes-based system for assessing the quality of the work providers perform for you? Do your assessments drive decisions about future hiring?
Are you revising your business model in order to manage smaller projects at acceptable profit? Is this activity looked down on in your firm?
Is your firm changing (at least) as rapidly as your most demanding clients?

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Christensen, Wang and van Bever predict that improving AI and big-data capabilities will accelerate the productization of consulting.
pts.d: This October 2013 article is primarily about management consulting, with legal services used as an analogy. The authors describe software-delivered intellectual property replacing some bespoke, human-capital-intensive engagements. Asset-based consulting generally requires less human intervention and customization and can spread lower expenses over subscriptions or licence fees. They identify Narrative Science as an existing example of AI-generated analytics and readable insights. These are claims about consulting technology in 2013, not about modern generative AI or measured AI performance in legal work.

pts.k: The authors claim that automated analytics can substitute for junior analytical work and deliver certain insights faster and more cheaply than traditional consulting teams.
pts.d: They state that BeyondCore's automated data analysis and animated briefings render the junior analyst role obsolete, and describe Motista's predictive customer insights as costing a small fraction of top-firm consulting prices. They also report that average costing and pricing analysis have already been automated and increasingly brought in-house. The junior-role statement is the authors' assertion based on a product example, not a reported employment study.

pts.k: The authors predict that measurable analytics and democratized knowledge will weaken brand-based protection and shift competition toward modular providers.
pts.d: Their mechanism is reduced opacity: clients gain access to data and quantifiable outputs that make prestigious brands less necessary as proxies for quality. They suggest this may accelerate growth at emerging-market consulting firms such as Tata Consultancy Services and Infosys. More broadly, they predict consolidation and increased acquisitions as leaner, technology-enabled competitors move upmarket, while retaining a premium segment for complex, high-stakes bespoke advice. These are linked technology-and-business-model predictions rather than effects attributed exclusively to AI.

pts.k: The legal-services comparison describes technology-assisted unbundling and alternative staffing, not a specific prediction about AI replacing lawyers.
pts.d: The authors report that corporate general counsel are reallocating work to providers including Axiom and Lawyers on Demand, which combine technology, workflow changes and alternative staffing to lower costs. They describe LeClairRyan's lower-cost discovery practice and Axiom's multidisciplinary approach as examples of changing delivery models. These legal-market claims provide an analogy for consulting disruption; the article does not isolate AI's contribution to their results.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The consulting claims draw on qualitative research, disruption theory and named business examples, rather than AI benchmarks or quantified causal studies.
pts.d: The authors report a year of professional-services research, conversations with more than 50 industry leaders, clients and researchers, and a May 2013 Harvard Business School roundtable. Examples include McKinsey Solutions, Narrative Science, BeyondCore and Motista. Their interpretation of McKinsey Solutions as a disruption hedge is explicitly their inference. No comparative performance tests, numerical cost comparisons or workforce measurements are provided for the AI and automation examples.

pts.k: Legal-sector surveys support the article's account of anticipated unbundling and competitive pressure, but do not measure AI effects.
pts.d: The article cites AdvanceLaw surveys of general counsel and Altman Weil surveys of law-firm leaders. Their results concern respondents' expectations or stated intentions, not demonstrated future outcomes: 52% anticipated greater use of temporary contract attorneys, 79% anticipated more unbundling, and 72% intended to move more work away from white-shoe firms. Altman Weil's 2009–2012 comparisons show increasing expectations of price competition, fewer equity partners and nonhourly billing. The supplied text does not report survey sample sizes or methods.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The authors see disruption as already beginning in 2013, but give no fixed deadline for AI-driven productization or industry restructuring.
pts.d: They explicitly limit current productization to a subset of consulting jobs and condition expansion on new intellectual property and improving AI and big-data capabilities. Technology-based delivery is most applicable to well-defined, repeatable, data-heavy analyses requiring regular updates. They acknowledge uncertainty about disruption's precise course and preserve a role for expensive bespoke advice on complex, interdependent, high-stakes problems.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are consulting analysts, incumbent partnerships, technology-enabled entrants and corporate buyers; the legal analogy concerns corporate legal departments and their providers.
pts.d: Junior analysts face the substitution claim. Incumbent consultancies face reduced differentiation, commoditization and competition between traditional engagements and software offerings. Modular and analytics providers gain entry opportunities, initially including smaller clients and subsequently larger corporations. Buyers gain cheaper, more controllable and repeatable services, while those facing high-stakes ambiguous problems may continue paying premium firms. In law, general counsel gain sourcing options, alternative providers gain work, and traditional firms face price and staffing pressure. The article does not make claims about individual access to justice.
